definition.text: A lack of fresh water sources, local or affordably transported, that can meet a region's normal demand for water.

facts.text: Experts distinguish two types: physical water scarcity and economic water scarcity.
Globally there is enough fresh water; scarcity comes from a mismatch between when and where people need water and when and where it is available.
Population growth, changing diets and living conditions, and expanding irrigated agriculture can cause it, as can climate change, deforestation, water pollution and wasteful use.
Half a billion people live with severe water scarcity all year, and around four billion face it for at least one month a year.
Of the 1.4 billion cubic kilometers of water on Earth, the UN estimates only 200,000 cubic kilometers is freshwater available for people.
Heavy water use in agriculture, livestock breeding and industry is the main consumption-driven cause of scarcity.
Responses include supply and demand management, cooperation between countries, water conservation, reusing wastewater and desalination.
In 2019 the World Economic Forum named water scarcity one of the largest global risks by potential impact over the next decade.

definition.text: Water scarcity that occurs when natural water resources are not enough to meet all demands, including the water ecosystems need.

facts.text: Dry regions, such as those with a desert climate, often suffer from it.
Central Asia, West Asia, North Africa and most of Australia are examples of arid areas.
Around a fifth of the world's population lives in regions affected by physical water scarcity.
The two-type distinction was first defined in a 2007 study led by the International Water Management Institute on 50 years of farm water use.

definition.text: Water scarcity caused by too little investment in the infrastructure or technology needed to draw water from rivers, aquifers and other sources.

facts.text: It also reflects weak human capacity to meet water demand.
The UN Development Programme says it is the most common cause of water scarcity, because most regions have enough water but lack the means to deliver it.
A quarter of the world's population is affected, much of Sub-Saharan Africa among them.
People without reliable access may travel long distances to fetch water, which is often unclean.

definition.text: Simple measures of how scarce water is, such as the ratio of water use to water available or the water available per person each year.

facts.text: The Falkenmark Water Stress Indicator counts water stress below 1,700 cubic meters per person per year and water scarcity below 1,000 cubic meters.
The FAO defines water stress as total freshwater withdrawn divided by total renewable freshwater minus environmental flow requirements.
Under that definition, below 10% is low stress and above 80% is very high stress.
Country averages hide uneven rainfall and access, so they can misstate scarcity.

definition.text: The branch of forestry that handles the administrative, legal, economic and social side of running forests, along with technical work such as silviculture and forest protection.

facts.text: Forests can be managed for timber, recreation, water, wildlife, wood products, genetic resources and other values, aiming at conservation, use or a mix of both.
Techniques include timber extraction, planting and replanting, building forest roads and paths, and preventing fire.
Forests supply water, slow climate change, shelter pollinators, provide timber, fuelwood, food and medicine, and support rural livelihoods.
Some forests are run only for firewood, paper fiber and timber, but managing for multiple uses is becoming more common as environmental awareness grows.
In 2025, 1.20 billion ha of forest (29% of all forest) was managed mainly for wood and non-wood products, and about 616 million ha was designated for multiple use.
Management intensity ranges from leaving a forest alone to intensive silvicultural regimes, raised to meet economic or ecological goals.
Modern scientific forestry arose from the 1750s in France and German-speaking countries, built on central management by professional foresters and sustainable yield.

definition.text: Managing forests according to the principles of sustainable development.

facts.text: It must balance three pillars: ecological, economic and sociocultural.
Its benefits range from protecting local livelihoods and biodiversity to reducing rural poverty and easing some effects of climate change.
The Forest Principles adopted at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit captured the international understanding of it at that time.
Forest under management plans grew by 365 million ha since 1990 to 2.13 billion ha, 55% of all forest in 2025.
Biodiversity conservation is the main aim in around 13% of the world's forests, and protecting soil and water in more than 30%.

definition.text: Protecting existing natural forests so they keep growing, storing carbon and gaining structural complexity without harvesting.

facts.text: It complements afforestation, reforestation and improved forest management as forest-based climate solutions.
Counting land clearing and short product lifetimes, plantations sequester 40 times less carbon than natural forests.
Old-growth and complex forests resist climate change effects and fire better than young forests.

definition.text: Growing forests planted for high-volume wood production, usually as a monoculture of one tree species.

facts.text: Plantations can produce a lot of wood in a short time.
Industrial plantations are large, actively managed, and made of even-aged blocks of one or two species.
Plantations may support fewer pollinators than structurally diverse natural forests.

title: Land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF)
article: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: A greenhouse gas inventory sector covering emissions and removals from direct human land use, land-use change and forestry.

facts.text: These activities can add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere or remove it, which influences climate.
UNFCCC guidelines require human-caused emissions to be reported in six sectors, LULUCF among them.
The Kyoto Protocol made accounting for afforestation, reforestation and deforestation mandatory, and for forest, cropland and grazing management voluntary.
Land-use, land-use change and forestry emissions averaged 1.1 ± 0.7 Gt C per year (4.1 ± 2.6 Gt CO2) over 2014–2023.
Land-use change also alters albedo and evapotranspiration, both of which affect climate.
A 2021 study found land-use change affected 17% of land in 1960–2019, with global trade affecting agriculture as a main driver.

conflicts.text: IPCC estimates land-use change contributes a net 1.6 ± 0.8 Gt carbon per year.
conflicts.note: Older IPCC estimate versus updated 2014–2023 average; different periods.

sources.title: Land use, land-use change, and forestry
sources.key: Land use, land-use change, and forestry

definition.text: The various ways of setting a price for water.

facts.text: Efficient pricing needs to know water's value in other uses, the private and external costs of supply, and the options for setting a tariff.
Tariffs can be uniform or variable and flat or volumetric, giving almost endless combinations.
Utility tariffs for piped water are set administratively and range from US$0.01 to almost US$8 per cubic meter.
Irrigation water is usually charged a flat rate because metering is uncommon in farming.
Raising irrigation prices does not always cut use proportionally, especially when farmers lack money, efficient technology or other livelihoods.
Some places let water rights be traded so the price forms in a market, as in parts of Australia, Chile and the Southwestern United States.

definition.text: Fees some countries levy for taking water directly from rivers, lakes and aquifers, which in most countries is free.

facts.text: They are typically charged to industries, utilities and farmers.
Few countries outside the OECD charge them, and where they exist fees are often nominal or poorly enforced.
Agriculture, the largest water user worldwide, is exempt in almost all countries that charge them.

definition.text: Natural sources of water that are potentially useful to people, for example for drinking or irrigation.

facts.text: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water and 3% fresh, and slightly over two-thirds of the fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice caps.
Most unfrozen fresh water is groundwater, with only a small fraction above ground or in the air.
Natural sources include surface water, flow beneath rivers, groundwater and frozen water.
Artificial sources include reclaimed wastewater, desalinated seawater, rainwater harvesting, wells, dams and reservoirs.
The only natural input to a surface water system is precipitation within its watershed.
Climate change brings heavier rain and floods, while droughts can shrink groundwater storage and recharge.

definition.text: How water is divided among uses such as irrigated farming, industry and households, some needing water only at times and others continuously.

facts.text: An estimated 22% of the world's water is used in industry, including power plant cooling, refineries and manufacturing.
About 8% is used for domestic purposes such as drinking, cooking, bathing and cleaning.
Industry may withdraw a lot of water but generally consumes much less than agriculture.
Irrigation has been central to agriculture for over 5,000 years.

definition.text: Planning, developing, distributing and managing the best use of water resources.

facts.text: Ideally it allocates water fairly among all competing demands, but in practice decision-makers must put sustainability, equity and optimisation first, in that order.
Climate change adds uncertainty, so participatory approaches and adaptive capacity are increasingly used.
Sustainable Development Goal 6 aims to implement integrated water resources management at all levels by 2030.
Many water bodies are shared across national or internal borders, which complicates fair management.

definition.text: A process that coordinates the development and management of water, land and related resources to maximize economic and social welfare fairly without harming vital ecosystems.

facts.text: It rests on three principles: social equity, economic efficiency and ecological sustainability.
It emerged at international conferences in the late 1900s and early 2000s and was recommended in the 1992 Dublin Statement.
Scholars see water security as the goal and IWRM as the process to reach it.
It is evolving to include the nexus approach, which recognizes that water, energy and food are closely linked.
There is no single correct administrative model; practice depends on context.

definition.text: Four principles for water management set out in the 1992 Dublin Statement.

facts.text: They hold that fresh water is finite and vulnerable, that management should be participatory, and that women play a central role.
The fourth principle says water has economic value in all its competing uses and should be recognized as an economic good.
They have guided reform of national water law around the world since 1992.

definition.text: A formula giving the present value of the income from repeatedly growing and harvesting a forest, used to find the best age to cut it.

facts.text: German forester Martin Faustmann derived it in 1849.
Because timber is renewable, waiting longer for a bigger harvest has a cost: it delays replanting and the next rotation.
It values the forest as pf(T) times the sum of discounted future harvests, PV = pf(T)/(exp(rT) − 1), where r is the discount rate.
The best time to cut is when the forest's value grows at the rate of interest on the forest plus interest on the land.
Bertil Ohlin solved the maximization in 1921, giving the Faustmann–Ohlin theorem.
Because it accounts for the time value of money, the financially optimal rotation is usually shorter than the biologically optimal one.
It remains widely used in natural resource valuation and policy analysis.

definition.text: A description of what happens on a piece of land: the benefits people get from it and the management actions they carry out there.

facts.text: The IPCC groups land into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands.
As of 2015, arable land was 10.7% of the land surface, with 1.3% permanent cropland.
Land use strongly affects water, soil, nutrients, plants and animals.
Its effects include urban sprawl, soil erosion, land degradation and desertification.
Governments often plan and regulate land use, for example by zoning, to avoid land-use conflicts.

definition.text: The change of a piece of land from one land-use category to another.

facts.text: Together with fossil fuel use, it is a major human source of carbon dioxide.
Human activity is the biggest cause of land cover change, and people also feel its environmental consequences.
Deforestation has historically been a main driver; global forest cover has shrunk by 35% since farming began.
Urban areas cover just 3% of Earth's surface but drive land change elsewhere through rising consumption.
A Soviet irrigation diversion cost the Aral Sea 85% of its area and 90% of its volume, wrecking its fishery.

definition.text: Public rules, such as zoning, by which governments plan and control how land may be used.

facts.text: An urban growth boundary is one form of land-use regulation.
New York City passed the first US zoning ordinance in 1916, and most states had zoning laws by the 1930s.
Most controls on land in the US actually come from private developers and individuals.

title: Virtual water

definition.text: The water hidden in food and other goods, which in effect moves from place to place when those goods are traded.

facts.text: It is also called embedded or embodied water; Tony Allan coined the concept in 1993 and won the Stockholm Water Prize for it in 2008.
A country that imports one tonne of wheat instead of growing it saves about 1,300 cubic meters of its own water.
Cereal imports can make up for local water shortages, but poor countries may not be able to afford them in future.
Water-scarce Israel discourages exporting water-intensive oranges to avoid exporting large amounts of water.
Virtual water data can be built into trade models such as the GTAP computable general equilibrium model to study water policy and trade.
Averaged worldwide, beef carries 15,497 cubic meters of virtual water per tonne, against 1,334 for wheat.

contested_note: Critics such as Australia's National Water Commission say measuring virtual water has little practical value for deciding how to allocate scarce water.

conflicts.text: It takes 1,340 cubic meters of water, on world average, to produce one tonne of wheat.
conflicts.note: Table gives a world average of 1,334 m3/ton and the Concept section about 1,300; likely rounding/edition differences.

verification.title: John Anthony Allan’s “Virtual Water”: Natural Resources Management in the Wake of Neoliberalism

definition.text: An underground layer of porous, permeable or fractured rock, or of gravel, sand or silt, that holds water.

facts.text: People can tap aquifers through wells for drinking water, farming and industry.
Aquifers are not underground rivers or lakes but porous rock saturated with water.
An aquitard is a layer of clay or non-porous rock that restricts groundwater flow between aquifers.
Taking out more water than is replenished exceeds the aquifer's practical sustained yield.
Challenges include overdrafting, land subsidence, salinization and pollution of groundwater.
In the arid parts of the Ogallala Aquifer, annual recharge is only about 10 percent of annual withdrawals.

definition.text: A classification of aquifers by whether an impermeable layer lies above them.

facts.text: An unconfined aquifer has no impermeable barrier above it, so its water level can rise with recharge; its top is the water table.
A confined aquifer has an impermeable layer above it that stops its water level rising.
The same rock unit may be confined in one place and unconfined in another.

title: Clearcutting

definition.text: A logging practice in which most or all of the trees in an area are cut down at once.

facts.text: It is the most economically efficient way to log, and is also used to clear land for farming.
It mimics the start of forest regrowth after a fire or windthrow and favors fast-growing, sun-loving tree species.
Variants include standard, patch and strip clearcuts and clearcutting with reserves.
It differs from selective logging, where only a few trees per hectare are harvested.
Removing trees reduces water retention, which can worsen flooding and wash nutrients out of the soil.
One study found clear-cut zones had nearly three times the erosion from slides, about five times once logging roads were counted.
Its long-run effects depend on how well the forest is managed and whether the land is converted to other uses.

contested_note: Loggers and forest-worker unions defend it on scientific, safety and economic grounds, while critics call it deforestation that destroys habitat; the costs of side effects like topsoil loss are intensely debated.

title: Commodification of water

definition.text: The process of turning water, especially fresh water, from a public good into a commodity that can be bought and sold.

facts.text: It is usually done in the hope that the resource will be managed more efficiently.
It grew sharply during the 20th century alongside concern about water scarcity and environmental damage.
Its theoretical case draws on Garrett Hardin's Tragedy of the Commons: water as a common good has been overused and poorly managed.
Putting a price on water aims to bring the costs of using it into economic decisions, on the logic that a correctly valued resource can be protected.
For most of the 20th century water was publicly provided by the state, with the emphasis on social equity.
Critics argue that the poor lose out as equality and universal access are traded for efficiency and profit.
Karen Bakker argues full commodification is nearly impossible because water's physical traits resist standardization.

contested_note: Proponents say markets allocate and protect water better than regulation; critics say commodification deepens inequality and harms ecosystems.

title: Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management
article: Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management

definition.text: Policy tools for evaluating and reporting how sustainably forests are managed in a country or region.

facts.text: Criteria set the objectives; indicators are the variables that show whether they are being met.
The idea dates to the 1992 Forest Principles and Agenda 21 adopted at the UN Conference on Environment and Development.
The Pan-European set has 6 criteria, such as forest health and biodiversity; the Montréal Process set has 7 criteria and 54 indicators.
They also help develop forest certification standards.

sources.title: Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management
sources.key: Criteria and indicators of sustainable forest management

definition.text: An area of land in which all flowing surface water drains to a single point, such as a river mouth, or into another body of water such as a lake or ocean.

facts.text: Ridges and hills form the drainage divide that separates one basin from the next.
It is also called a watershed in North America, or a catchment or river basin.
Most water leaving a basin's outlet fell on it as precipitation.
Because basins are coherent hydrological units, water resources are commonly managed basin by basin.
Water carries nutrients, sediment and pollutants to the basin outlet; fertilizer runoff can cause eutrophication there.
The Amazon basin is the largest at 7 million km2, followed by the Congo and the Nile.
A basin crossing a political border is a transboundary river, managed jointly by the countries sharing it.

definition.text: An inland drainage basin whose water never reaches the ocean.

facts.text: Endorheic basins cover around 18% of Earth's land.
Where evaporation is the main loss, their water is usually saltier than the ocean, the Dead Sea being an extreme case.
The largest are in Central Asia, including the Caspian and Aral Seas.

definition.text: Features of a drainage basin, namely topography, shape, size, soil type and land use, that determine how likely it is to flood.

facts.text: Topography and shape set how fast rain reaches the river; size, soil and development set how much arrives.
Sandy soils absorb rain while clay soils are nearly impermeable and add to flood volumes.
Rain on roofs, pavements and roads reaches rivers with almost no absorption into groundwater.

definition.text: The amount, timing and quality of river flow needed to sustain freshwater and estuarine ecosystems and the people who depend on them.

facts.text: Managers aim for a flow pattern that serves human uses while keeping river ecosystems healthy, not necessarily restoring pristine flows.
More than half of the world's large rivers are dammed, and dams change downstream water quality, temperature, sediment, fish and livelihoods.
The idea grew from 1970s 'minimum flows' for single species such as trout, then 'instream flows'.
By the 1990s scientists saw that one minimum flow could not capture river systems.
The 2007 Brisbane Declaration was endorsed by more than 750 practitioners from more than 50 countries.
More than 200 methods exist; holistic ones include DRIFT, the Building Block Methodology and ELOHA.
Dam reoperation combined with floodplain restoration has sometimes increased hydropower water while reducing flood risk.

definition.text: Food that is thrown away or otherwise lost without being eaten.

facts.text: It happens at every stage of the food system, but most food waste arises after consumers buy food.
About one-third of the world's food is thrown away, wasting the resources used to produce it.
Global food waste is 931 million tonnes a year (about 121 kg per person): 61 percent from households, 26 percent from food service and 13 percent from retail.
Wasted food accounts for 3.3 billion tons of CO2-equivalent emissions a year, and landfilled food is a major methane source.
The FAO defines it as a decrease in the quantity or quality of food along the supply chain; definitions of loss versus waste vary.
Reducing it brings social gains, such as productivity, food security and lower environmental impact, that individual actors may not take into account.
The SDGs aim to halve per capita retail and consumer food waste by 2030.

title: Net animal losses
article: Food loss and waste#Net animal losses

definition.text: A measure of food waste: the calories in human-edible crops fed to animals minus the calories returned as meat, dairy and fish.

facts.text: These losses are higher than all conventional food losses combined.
Measuring loss in tonnes ignores economic value and can overweight heavy, low-value products.

definition.text: All the connected people, institutions, policies and infrastructure involved in feeding a population.

facts.text: It covers production, processing, packaging, distribution, marketing, consumption and disposal of food waste.
Conventional food systems run on economies of scale, specialization, long supply chains and global trade to cut unit costs.
They have raised productivity and food availability but are linked to soil degradation, biodiversity loss, greenhouse gas emissions and unequal access to food.
Since 1961, food supply per person has risen by more than 30%.
The food system causes more than a third (34%) of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Conventional systems depend heavily on cheap fossil fuels for machinery, fertilizer and processing.

definition.text: The environmental, social and health costs of producing and eating food that are not reflected in food prices, also called external costs.

facts.text: Examples include food's contribution to climate change, farmworker poverty and diet-related illness, all paid for by society.
Estimates of the total hidden costs of global agrifood systems range from USD 12 trillion to USD 19 trillion per year.
Hidden health costs amount to USD 8.1 trillion.
Greenhouse gas costs are fairly easy to measure; effects on working conditions and communities are harder.

definition.text: A food system that provides healthy food while sustaining the environmental, economic and social systems around food.

facts.text: It starts from sustainable farming and distribution, sustainable diets and less food waste.
Around 69 million hectares a year grow food that is lost or wasted before reaching consumers.
Sustainable food systems are argued to be central to many or all 17 SDGs.

definition.text: Initiatives that organize food production, distribution and eating differently from conventional industrial systems.

facts.text: They include farmers' markets, community-supported agriculture, food cooperatives and buying groups.
They are marked by locality, short supply chains and direct links between producers and consumers.
Fair trade aims to give developing-country producers more control and a bigger share of the sale price.

definition.text: Any material taken from forestry for direct use or sale, such as lumber, paper or livestock fodder.

facts.text: Wood is by far the main product, used as fuel, building material and pulp for paper.
All other products from forests are grouped as non-timber forest products, seen as less harmful to forest ecosystems while giving local income.
In 2023, global exports of wood and paper products were worth US$482 billion.
Industrial roundwood removals were 1.92 billion cubic meters and sawnwood production 445 million cubic meters.
Wood products store carbon, and timber can replace concrete as a recyclable building material.
Burning bioenergy initially emits more greenhouse gas per unit of energy than fossil fuels; regrowing trees takes decades or centuries to reabsorb it.
Access restrictions, harvesting fees and harvest limits are policies that shape forest product economics.

definition.text: The science and craft of creating, managing, planting, using, conserving and repairing forests and woodlands for human and environmental benefit.

facts.text: It is practiced in plantations and natural stands, and its practitioner is a forester.
Modern forestry practices multiple-use management: timber, fuel wood, wildlife habitat, water quality, recreation, jobs and more.
Managing forests for timber is silviculture, though the two terms are often used as synonyms.
Forests provide more than 86 million green jobs, and an estimated 880 million people collect firewood or make charcoal.
Policy tends to favor market benefits like timber, prompting frameworks that count non-market ecosystem services too.
Some 252 million people living in forests and savannahs earn less than US$1.25 a day.
Logging has a fatality rate 30 times higher than all other US occupations.

definition.text: The DNA differences among forest trees, which keep forests healthy and able to adapt.

facts.text: It gives resilience to pests and diseases and lets trees survive and evolve as conditions change.
It is threatened by fire, habitat fragmentation, pests, poor silviculture and unsuitable planting material.

definition.text: Water held beneath Earth's surface in the pore spaces of soil and rock and in rock fractures.

facts.text: About 30 percent of readily available fresh water, and about 99% of the world's liquid fresh water, is groundwater.
The water table is the depth at which soil or rock becomes completely saturated with water.
Groundwater is recharged from the surface and discharges naturally at springs and seeps.
It supplies about half of the world's drinking water, 40% of irrigation water and a third of industrial water.
It acts as natural storage that buffers against surface water shortages in drought.
Deep groundwater that infiltrated millennia ago is called fossil water.
Contaminants such as arsenic, fluoride and salt can make groundwater unsuitable to drink.

definition.text: Sinking or collapse of the ground when too much water is pumped out from underground.

facts.text: Groundwater pressure in the pores normally helps support the weight of the sediments above.
One estimate links 80% of serious US land subsidence problems to excessive groundwater extraction.
Subsidence can permanently reduce an aquifer's storage capacity.

definition.text: The movement of dense seawater into coastal aquifers, which hold a lens of fresh water on top of salt water.

facts.text: In sandy coastal aquifers, fresh water sits about 12 metres thick above salt water for every 0.3 m of freshwater head above sea level.
Overpumping lowers aquifer pressure and lets salt water in, and a salted aquifer can no longer reliably supply towns.

definition.text: Contamination that happens when pollutants released on the ground make their way into groundwater.

facts.text: Sources include on-site sanitation, landfill leachate, leaking sewers, petrol stations, fracking and overuse of farm fertilizer.
Using deep, confined aquifers gives more protection from surface contamination.

definition.text: Pumping groundwater out faster than an aquifer's equilibrium yield, also called overdrafting.

facts.text: Excessive pumping is the main cause, and insufficient recharge makes the aquifer less useful.
Safe yield is what can be withdrawn without exceeding long-term recharge; sustainable yield also accounts for impacts on surface water.
Pumping creates a cone of depression around a well that widens as extraction continues.
Overdrafting lowers the water table, shrinks streams, wetlands and lakes, and can cause subsidence and saltwater intrusion.
Roughly 40% of global irrigation relies on groundwater, and irrigation is the main cause of storage loss in the US.
About 800 km3 of US groundwater was depleted during the 20th century.
Remedies include artificial recharge, better governance, conservation incentives and more efficient farming.

definition.text: The unequal economic burden created as falling water tables force users to dig deeper wells.

facts.text: In Punjab, the cost of deeper wells hurt small landholders more than large ones, who could afford the technology.
Prior appropriation rights let established, richer users keep their water while newcomers and small farmers get less.

definition.text: Harvesting, transporting, buying or selling timber in breach of the law.

facts.text: It includes logging without permission, in protected areas, of protected species, or beyond agreed limits, often through corruption.
Fraudulent customs declarations, tax avoidance and fake certification during trade are called wood laundering.
Demand for raw materials, land grabbing and demand for cattle pasture drive it.
Illegal logging on public land alone causes losses of over US$10 billion a year, and more than half of global logging may be illegal.
Governments tend to underestimate it while NGOs publish alarming figures, so estimates need caution.
It drives deforestation and biodiversity loss, fosters corruption and tax evasion, and cuts producer countries' revenue.
The EU's 2003 FLEGT Action Plan works mainly through Voluntary Partnership Agreements with timber-producing countries.

definition.text: Farming of crops or animals with high inputs and outputs per unit of land, as opposed to extensive farming.

facts.text: It uses little fallow and more capital, labour, agrochemicals and water to raise yields per hectare.
Most supermarket meat, dairy, eggs, fruit and vegetables come from intensive farms.
Raising productivity sustainably, especially on smallholdings, can reduce the land farming needs and slow deforestation.
Industrial agriculture causes 14–28% of net greenhouse gas emissions.
Its effects reach far from farms: Midwest nitrogen travels down the Mississippi to create dead zones in the Gulf of Mexico.
Crop irrigation accounts for 70% of the world's fresh water use.
Enclosure, mechanization, four-field crop rotation and selective breeding drove Britain's farm productivity rise from the 16th to 19th centuries.

definition.text: Raising livestock in confinement at high density, often called factory farming.

facts.text: Such operations may hold up to hundreds of thousands of cows, hogs, turkeys or chickens, often indoors.
They aim for maximum output at the lowest cost and have greatly increased animal food production.

contested_note: Critics call the deals a form of neocolonialism, while host governments present them as development, and estimates of their scale disagree.
title: Land grabbing

definition.text: The large-scale buying or leasing of land by domestic or foreign companies, governments and individuals.

facts.text: In the 21st century the term mainly refers to large land acquisitions that followed the 2007–08 world food price crisis.
The crisis set off a sharp rise in mostly foreign agricultural investment in the Global South to grow industrial food and biofuels.
Securing water is usually central to these deals, which has produced a related trend called water grabbing.
Investors fall into three broad types: agribusinesses, governments and speculative investors.
Food-driven deals make up roughly 37% of land investments worldwide, and biofuel production about 21%.
Estimates of the area involved vary: the World Bank reported 46 million ha announced by 2010, while a 2011 estimate put it above 80 million ha; one 2013 review warned the scale may be exaggerated.
Critics point to weak land tenure, poor consultation, displacement of local people without adequate compensation, and the turn to large-scale industrial farming.
A World Bank study estimated that only 2 to 10 percent of land in Africa is formally tenured, which leaves many users exposed.

definition.text: A tax on the value of land alone, ignoring buildings and other improvements on it.

facts.text: Many economists favor it, arguing that it does not cause economic inefficiency and helps reduce inequality.
Most taxes discourage useful activity; property taxes, for example, discourage building and repair because the tax rises with improvements.
Because the amount of land is fixed, the tax cannot be passed on to tenants, consumers or workers, so it falls on landowners, who tend to be rich.
It removes the reward for holding unused land just to wait for its price to rise, freeing more land for productive use.
It is hard to evade, since land cannot be hidden or moved abroad and titles are publicly registered.
Supporters argue that land value comes from its surroundings rather than from anything the owner does.
Adam Smith first analyzed it rigorously in 1776, and Henry George later campaigned for a single tax on land to replace all other taxes.
Levying it requires a land valuation and a title register, and it is impractical where land titles and tenure are uncertain.

contested_note: Sources agree regulation changes how land is used but dispute whether the changes are beneficial, with critics blaming strict rules for housing shortages.
title: Land-use planning

definition.text: The process by which a central authority regulates how land may be used.

facts.text: It is usually done to get better social and environmental outcomes and to use resources more efficiently.
Modern goals often include conserving the environment, restraining urban sprawl, cutting transport costs, preventing land-use conflicts and reducing exposure to pollutants.
It nearly always relies on land-use regulation, typically zoning, which controls what activities may happen on a piece of land and how buildings are placed and shaped.
Green belts and urban growth boundaries are common tools for protecting rural and farm land from development spreading out of cities.
Planners assume regulation changes behavior, which is widely accepted, but whether those changes are beneficial is contested and depends on place and rules.
Critics say rules are often too strict, making land supply too inelastic and pushing prices up sharply; in North America planning systems have worsened housing crises.
Non-structural flood management includes land-use planning alongside warning systems and flood insurance.

notes: Article is a single-country (US) law; drafted as the general principle it defines. Consider merging into Sustainable forest management if judged too national.
title: Multiple use and sustained yield

definition.text: A forest management principle, written into a 1960 United States law, of using a forest's timber, range, water, recreation and wildlife together while keeping their output going indefinitely.

facts.text: Multiple use means managing all a forest's renewable surface resources in the combination that best meets people's needs.
Sustained yield means keeping a high regular output of renewable resources forever without harming the land's productivity.
The 1960 act was the first law to treat the five major uses of national forests equally, with timber sales no longer always the limiting factor.

definition.text: A way of raising livestock by letting the animals graze on large open pastures, historically by nomadic people who moved with their herds.

facts.text: It is practised where dryness, poor soils, extreme temperatures or lack of water make growing crops difficult or impossible.
As of 2019 between 200 million and 500 million people practised pastoralism, and 75% of all countries had pastoral communities.
Pastoralists manage rangelands covering about a third of Earth's land surface, producing food where crops cannot grow.
Mobile forms range from short daily moves, to transhumance between seasonal pastures, to fully nomadic herding.
Enclosure of common land, harder borders, fences and expanding crop farming have made settled pastoralism more common.
One review of many studies found pastoralism 2 to 10 times more productive per unit of land than capital-intensive alternatives, yet policies often try to replace it.
Grazing on savannas and woodlands can help keep their biodiversity and stop them turning into dense shrubland or forest.
Because they work marginal land in extreme environments, pastoral communities are very vulnerable to global warming.

contested_note: Hardin's view that pastoral commons inevitably degrade is disputed by Ostrom and many other scholars.
title: Pastoral commons and Hardin's critique

definition.text: The dispute over whether shared grazing lands are bound to be overused, as Garrett Hardin argued in 1968, or can be governed well by communities, as Elinor Ostrom showed.

facts.text: Hardin treated pastoralist land use as unstable and a cause of environmental degradation, and his paper gave a basis for privatizing land.
Many scholars call his assumption that herders cannot communicate or make agreements implausible, yet it shaped development projects that broke up working pastoral governance, often disastrously.
Ostrom argued grazing commons can be managed more sustainably by community groups and cooperatives than by privatization or full state control.

definition.text: The idea that the availability, quality and use of fresh water face growing limits.

facts.text: Peter Gleick and Meena Palaniappan defined it in 2010, separating peak renewable, peak non-renewable and peak ecological water.
Their point is that although the planet holds a vast amount of water, sustainably managed water is becoming scarce.
Of an estimated 1.34 billion cubic kilometres of water on Earth, 96.5% is salty and less than 1% is accessible to people.
Agriculture accounts for 70% of freshwater use worldwide.
Fossil water behaves like oil: pumping it faster than natural recharge can in theory give a Hubbert-type production peak.
The Ogallala Aquifer is mined far faster than it refills, a classic case of peak non-renewable water.
Saudi Arabia reached peak water in the early 1990s at more than 30 billion cubic metres a year and now produces about half that peak rate.
Typically only 35% to 50% of water withdrawn for irrigation reaches the crops, and higher water prices have been shown to improve efficiency of use.

definition.text: Water sources, such as desalinated seawater, that can replace unsustainable or non-renewable water use, usually at a higher cost.

facts.text: A backstop resource is one abundant and sustainable enough to replace a non-renewable one, as renewable energy is for fossil fuels.
Desalination is the classic backstop; transfers between river basins and trucked water are others, and all are last-resort, expensive options.
Desalination is limited by its energy needs, brine disposal, high capital and water costs, and the cost of moving water.
Desalination cost US$0.53 per cubic metre in Israel in 2005 and US$0.49 in Singapore in 2006.

definition.text: A farm management strategy that collects and analyzes data on fields, plants and animals to tailor decisions to local variation and use resources more efficiently.

facts.text: It applies precise amounts of water, fertilizer and pesticides at the right time, and can cut inputs while raising yields.
Farmers earn back their investment by saving on water, pesticide and fertilizer; targeting inputs also benefits soils and groundwater.
It relies on GPS, geographic information systems, variable-rate technology, grid sampling and remote sensing.
The idea first emerged in the United States in the early 1980s.

notes: National (US) doctrine, but it is one of the two main water-rights systems named on Water trading and Water right pages.
title: Prior-appropriation water rights

definition.text: A rule for sharing water under which the first person to take water for a beneficial use keeps the right to go on taking that amount for that use.

facts.text: It is often summed up as "first in time, first in right"; later users may take only what is left without harming earlier users.
It gives a right to withdraw water, not full ownership, and the right can be lost if left unused for a long time.
Rights are first allotted by date of use and can then be traded on the open market like other property.
Each year the holder with the earliest date takes their full allocation first, then the next, and in a shortage senior users need not cut back.
It arose in Gold-Rush-era California and spread to the arid western United States, where water is scarce.
Because users who leave part of their allotment unused risk losing it, the rule discourages conservation, and most western water still goes to agriculture.
Streams can become over-appropriated, holding more rights than there is water, so the newest users almost never receive any.
The doctrine has historically excluded ecological uses such as keeping water in a river for wildlife, though some jurisdictions now accept them.

definition.text: The use of the first in time, first in right principle for resources other than water, such as mineral deposits, farmland and pollution rights.

facts.text: Gold Rush miners applied it to mineral deposits: the first to find and mine a deposit gained the legal right to mine it.
Granting pollution rights to existing polluters, from which a cap-and-trade market could develop, would apply the same theory to air pollution.
Carbon markets that let firms offset new emissions against cuts at existing sources in effect recognize a prior right of existing emitters.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether reduced-impact logging is financially worse or better for loggers than conventional logging.
title: Reduced-impact logging

definition.text: A set of carefully planned and controlled timber-harvesting practices, carried out by trained workers, that make selective logging of tropical forests less damaging.

facts.text: Selective logging removes only a few species of trees above a minimum size and leaves the rest standing, unlike clearcutting.
Selective logging is estimated to affect 1 billion hectares of forest worldwide, including 680 million hectares of tropical forest.
Done by untrained, poorly supervised crews too often or too heavily, selective logging badly damages the stand, water functions and biodiversity.
The term arose in the late 1990s after mechanized logging was seen to threaten long-term sustainability.
FAO's model code calls for a minimum 20-year cutting cycle, removing no more than one-third of stand basal area, and directional felling.
It damages fewer trees and less soil, but in Southeast Asia logging more than 8 trees per hectare cancels its benefits.
Whether it costs loggers money is contested: studies show both losses and gains from less wasted timber.
It can earn rewards through carbon retention and payments for environmental services, and is an eligible REDD+ activity.

definition.text: A system that shares water among the owners of land along a river, lake or other water body.

facts.text: It comes from English common law and is used in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the eastern United States.
All owners whose land touches the water may make reasonable use of it; in a shortage, shares usually follow the length of each owner's frontage.
The rights cannot be sold apart from the land, and water cannot be moved out of the watershed without regard for downstream owners.
Downstream owners have a right to receive water undiminished in flow and quality.
In the United States the arid western states mainly follow prior appropriation, while the eastern states follow riparian law.

contested_note: Sources dispute how far shifting cultivators, rather than logging and wider economic forces, are to blame for tropical deforestation.
title: Shifting cultivation

definition.text: A farming system in which a plot is cropped for a while, then left to regrow wild vegetation while the farmer moves on to another plot.

facts.text: Cropping usually stops when the soil tires or, more often, weeds take over, and the fallow period is usually longer than the cropping period.
Land is often cleared by slash-and-burn, and after two or three years of crops the plot is left for another.
Fallows are not idle: they supply timber, firewood, medicines and game, and tree fallows protect soil from erosion and lift nutrients from deep layers.
It was one of the first forms of farming, and it is still widespread in the tropical developing world.
Stable cycles are vulnerable to fast population growth and outside economic change; chain saws and cash crops have shortened fallows and lengthened cropping.

Shifting cultivators are often blamed for forest loss, but sources argue tropical deforestation is driven by the same forces that cleared Europe's forests: urbanization, industrialization, affluence and population growth.
FAO's naming of shifting cultivation, but not logging, as a cause of deforestation led to a clash with environmental groups.

definition.text: The practice of controlling how forests grow, what they are made of and their quality, mainly to produce timber.

facts.text: It works at the level of the individual stand of trees, whereas forestry is the broader field.
It is essentially the commercial business of growing forest crops, based on knowledge of how trees and stands live.
Regeneration can come from self-sown seed, artificially sown seed or planted seedlings.
Tending treats a crop after planting, by spacing, pruning and thinning trees or by weeding out competing vegetation.
Pruning lower branches lets clear, knot-free wood grow, which is worth more.
In 16th-century Germany landowners developed silviculture to deal with deforestation.
On old, poor soils or where dry-season fires threaten the crop, trees may grow too slowly for silviculture to pay.

definition.text: Cutting out some of the trees in a stand so that the remaining ones grow faster.

facts.text: Its aim is to control how much growing space each tree gets, shaping the growth, quality and health of those left.
Precommercial thinning of dense young stands can greatly raise the yield of saleable wood and shorten the rotation.
Repeated thinnings over a rotation have been shown to store more carbon than clear-cutting on short rotations.

definition.text: A way of regrowing a forest that relies on cut trees sending up new shoots from their stumps.

facts.text: Most hardwoods, the coast redwood and certain pines sprout from stumps and can be coppiced.
It is generally used to produce fuelwood, pulpwood and other small-tree products.
The three recognized systems are simple coppice, coppice with standards, where some fine trees are kept for several rotations, and the coppice selection system.

definition.text: The two broad families of methods that combine harvesting timber with re-establishing the forest, differing in how much of the stand is cut at once.

facts.text: Uneven-aged methods harvest single trees or small groups now and then, keeping mixed sizes and ages; even-aged methods remove most or all of the overstory, leaving a stand of one age.
The shelterwood system removes a stand through several partial cuts over years, ending in a new even-aged stand.
Selection systems suit places where keeping continuous forest cover for scenic or environmental reasons matters most.
Variable retention, a newer system, leaves stumps, logs, snags and live trees for at least one rotation to keep environmental values.

definition.text: A form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to make a field, called a swidden.

facts.text: The cut vegetation dries and is burned, leaving nutrient-rich ash that fertilizes the soil and briefly clears weeds and pests.
After about three to five years nutrients run down and weeds and pests invade, so farmers move on; recovery takes from five to more than twenty years.
A rough estimate is that 200–300 million people worldwide use it.
It has been used to clear land for crops and livestock since Neolithic times.
On the very poor, leached soils of places like the Amazon it is one of the few kinds of farming possible, and it has been sustainable for thousands of years.
It is sustainable only with a huge amount of land or few people, and is poorly suited to cash crops.
It is a common method of agricultural deforestation that has become less sustainable.
Replacing it with slash-and-char could offset up to 12% of human carbon emissions from land-use change each year (0.21 gigatonnes).

definition.text: Efforts to protect and restore tropical rainforests, ranging from strict preservation to sustainable management by people living in them.

facts.text: Its building blocks include ecotourism, rehabilitation, reforestation and restoration.
Approaches differ: Asian governments such as Vietnam and China fund planting directly, while Peru and Brazil give farmers incentives like tax credits to reduce deforestation.
Countries can earn carbon credits by conserving or replanting rainforest, making conservation pay economically.
The Bonn Challenge, signed in 2011 by 58 countries, pledged to restore 150 million hectares of forest by 2020, later raised to 350 Mha by 2030.

title: Restoration hotspots
article: Tropical rainforest conservation#Keys to successful restoration

definition.text: Areas where restoring rainforest gives the highest social and economic benefits and is most feasible.

facts.text: They matter because, for an individual landowner, clearing forest often pays more than keeping it.

Benefits are scored on biodiversity, climate mitigation, climate adaptation and water security; feasibility on the opportunity cost of taking land out of farming, the forest's ability to recover, and the chance it lasts.
By these criteria over 863 Mha of rainforest qualifies, nearly a third of it in Brazil.

definition.text: A state in which long overuse of a water system has caused damage so lasting that it can no longer return to its former supply and ecosystem services.

facts.text: It has two parts: withdrawals exceed renewable inflows and safe depletion limits, and the damage cannot be undone without disproportionate cost.
It differs from water scarcity, water stress and a water crisis, which may still be reversible, by stressing insolvency and lost recoverability.
Kaveh Madani formally defined it, and a United Nations University report of 20 January 2026 declared the world had entered a global water bankruptcy era.

contested_note: Proponents and opponents disagree on whether private participation improves access, efficiency and prices, and the evidence is mixed.
title: Water privatization

definition.text: The involvement of private companies in providing water supply and sanitation services.

facts.text: There are two broad forms: full privatization, where assets are sold permanently, and public–private partnerships, where the public keeps ownership and hands some functions to a firm for a set period.
Full privatization is now rare, limited to England, Chile and some US cities.
Supporters say it raises efficiency and service quality and can bring fiscal benefits; critics say it raises tariffs and conflicts with the human right to water.
Private utilities were common in the 19th century, faded as public utilities grew, and returned in the early 1990s, pushed partly by World Bank and IMF lending conditions.
Like all water utilities, private operators are monopolies and need regulation of tariffs, service quality and environmental compliance.
The evidence on its impact is mixed, and both sides tend to cite the studies that suit them.
A World Bank review found no statistically significant difference in efficiency between public and private operators.
A study of Latin American concessions found modest returns, averaging 7 percent a year on capital employed.

distinct_from: Human right to water and sanitation
notes: Overlaps Water resource management (Water resources#Water resource management, part03); the page itself says the terms are sometimes synonyms. Merge if judged duplicate.
title: Water resource policy

definition.text: The policy-making and laws that govern how water is collected, treated, used, disposed of and protected.

facts.text: It varies by region with water availability, the state of aquatic systems and local needs.
For policy, water is often sorted into blue water (surface and groundwater), green water (rain held in soil for plants), grey water (contaminated by use) and virtual water.
Drought frequency and intensity are rising with climate change, but water policy tends to react rather than plan ahead.

distinct_from: Human right to water and sanitation
title: Transboundary water agreements

definition.text: Treaties and other agreements between countries on how to share and manage water that crosses their borders.

facts.text: About 60% of the world's freshwater flows across political boundaries, because basins do not follow national borders.
An estimated 3600 water treaties have existed, more than 150 of them new since 1950.
Rivers that form a border and can be shared equally tend to cause less conflict than upstream–downstream arrangements.
Growing scarcity, climate change and poorer water quality have increased international conflict over water.

title: Human right to water and sanitation
article: Water resource policy#Human right to water and sanitation

definition.text: The principle that clean drinking water and sanitation are a universal human right because every life depends on them.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly recognized it as a human right on 28 July 2010.
Its clearest definition came in General Comment 15 of the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, drafted in 2002.
Only a few countries have written it into enforceable law.

definition.text: A user's legal right to take and use water from a source such as a river, stream, pond or groundwater.

facts.text: Where water is plentiful and users few, such rights are simple, but in dry irrigated areas they often cause legal and physical conflict.
Often they rest on owning the land the water touches, known as riparian rights, and are judged by a test of reasonable use.
Where water is scarcer, as in the western United States, rights follow prior appropriation: first in time, first in right.
Each appropriative right has an annual yield and a date, and it keeps that date when sold.
In ancient Rome people could gain temporary rights to running water that did not depend on owning land and lasted while use continued.
Over time rights broadened from land-based to use-based, letting non-landowners hold enforceable rights to clean water.
Some systems treat surface water and groundwater alike, while others apply different rules to each.

definition.text: The goal of getting the most benefit from water for people and ecosystems while keeping the risks of floods, droughts and polluted water acceptably low.

facts.text: People with high water security always have enough water of acceptable quality for health, livelihoods and production.
It emerged as a concept in the 21st century and is broader than the absence of water scarcity; some organizations use it only for water supply.
How easily a society sustains it depends on its hydrologic environment, its socio-economic environment and future climate change.
Its main threats are water scarcity, pollution and lower water quality from climate change, plus poverty, destructive floods and natural disasters.
About 27% of the world's population lived in water-scarce areas in the mid-2010s, likely rising to 42% by 2050.
Responses include engineering to raise supply or efficiency, financial safety nets for poorer people, and management tools such as demand caps.
There is no single or standard way to measure it; metrics are based either on household experiences or on water resources.
The IPCC predicted that 2 °C of global warming would expose roughly 1–4 billion people to water stress.

definition.text: The possibility of water-related problems such as scarcity, stress, flooding, drought or decaying infrastructure.

facts.text: Water risk and water security move in opposite directions: as risk rises, security falls.
Like other risks it combines hazard, exposure and vulnerability.
It threatens whole industries such as food and beverages, agriculture, oil and gas and utilities; agriculture uses 69% of the world's freshwater.

definition.text: Violence or disputes over access to or control of water, or the use of water and water systems as weapons or targets in conflicts.

facts.text: Conflicts are rarely wars over water alone; water is more often one cause of tension among several.
They can be interstate, between countries sharing a river, sea or aquifer, or intrastate, such as farmers against city users.
The Middle East has only 1% of the world's fresh water for 5% of its population, and most of its rivers cross borders.

definition.text: The two-way link between the water used to produce energy and the energy used to extract, treat, move, heat and dispose of water.

facts.text: Every form of energy production needs some water, and every stage of the water cycle needs energy, so the two cannot be separated.
Water is used when it is returned to its source, as in power-plant cooling, and consumed when it is removed by evaporation or by crops or people.
Thermoelectric power plants, which use water for cooling, are by far the largest users of water.
Some low-carbon options, such as biofuels, concentrating solar power, carbon capture and nuclear power, are quite water-intensive.
Gulf states spend 10–25% of their electricity on desalinating water.

definition.text: A branch of applied economics that uses economic theory to improve how food and fibre are produced and distributed.

facts.text: It began as a branch dealing with land use, aiming to maximize crop yields while keeping soils healthy.
It grew to prominence around the turn of the 20th century and made early contributions to econometric methods.

In environmental economics, agricultural economists design incentives to control externalities like farm water pollution and estimate the value of non-market benefits such as attractive rural landscapes.
The farm sector is often cited as a prime example of perfect competition.

definition.text: Useful foods, materials and other goods taken from forests other than timber.

facts.text: They include game, nuts, berries, mushrooms, oils, sap, medicinal plants, fuelwood, fish, insects, spices and forage, harvested from the wild or farmed.
Non-wood forest products are a subset that excludes woodfuel and charcoal; FAO estimated they generated US$88 billion in 2011.
Around 1 billion people depend to some extent on wild foods, and several million households rely on these products for income.
More than 28,000 plant species are recorded as medicinal, many of them from forests.
Their total economic value is hard to estimate because no broad system tracks the hundreds of products involved.
Research treats them as commodities that can make keeping forests pay, and in some places as a route out of poverty.
Community forestry often manages forests for income from both timber and non-timber products.

definition.text: Laws that govern activities on designated forest land, mainly forest management and timber harvesting.

facts.text: They usually set management policies for public forests such as multiple use and sustained yield.
They aim to protect resources and prevent clearing, logging, hunting and plant collecting, but often set no clear limits on allowable cuts or rotations.
Rules on forest use spanning generations are among the oldest long-term environmental policies, dating to customary law codified in the 14th century.
Since the Kyoto Protocol, climate change mitigation has become an objective of forest law and policy.

title: Von Thünen model

definition.text: Johann Heinrich von Thünen's model of farmland use, set out in The Isolated State (1826), in which the cost of transporting goods eats into the rent land can earn.

facts.text: It is considered the first example of marginal analysis and an early explicit, abstract model to which mathematics could be applied.
Von Thünen developed the spatial analysis of rents, stressing the importance of centrality and transport.
Its publication is said to mark the real start of location theory, and von Thünen has been called the father of location theorists.
Critics say it oversimplified the problem by assuming an isolated state or a single city.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; no crawled sentence describes the model's concentric land-use rings, so that core idea is listed as a gap.

definition.text: Agriculture is the cultivation of soil and the planting and harvesting of food and non-food crops, together with livestock production.

facts.text: Broader definitions also take in forestry and aquaculture, though horticulture and forestry are often left out in practice.
Farming created food surpluses that let people live in cities and let population grow far beyond what hunting and gathering could sustain.
Agriculture covers 4.8 billion ha, about one-third of the Earth's land, and affects land and water resources more than any other economic sector.
Agricultural expansion drives deforestation and degrades carbon-rich ecosystems such as peatlands; about 40% of agricultural land is seriously degraded.
Intensive agriculture raised yields by substituting synthetic fertilizers and pesticides for labour, but increased water pollution and often relied on subsidies.
Livestock occupy 70% of agricultural land, which is 30% of the planet's land surface.
Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
FAO estimates agriculture must produce about 50% more food, feed and fibre by 2050 than in 2012, adding pressure on water, land and soil.

definition.text: Bioenergy is renewable energy obtained by using biomass as fuel, whether wood, energy crops, harvest residues or organic waste.

facts.text: The IPCC defines bioenergy as energy from any form of biomass, meaning organic material excluding fossilised matter, so coal is not biomass here.
Traditional biomass is wood, charcoal, residues or dung burned for cooking or heating in open fires or inefficient stoves, common in low-income countries.
Wood and wood residues are the largest biomass energy source today; main waste feedstocks are wood, agricultural, municipal solid and manufacturing waste.
Biomass is upgraded by thermal, chemical or biochemical routes; thermal options are torrefaction, pyrolysis and gasification.
In the EU in 2023 bioenergy was about three-quarters of renewable heating and cooling and nearly one-fifth of all heating and cooling.
Over its life cycle bioenergy can emit less or more greenhouse gas than the energy it replaces, depending on how feedstock is grown, harvested and transported.

Bioenergy crops can displace natural ecosystems, degrade soils and use water and synthetic fertilisers; about one-third of wood for traditional tropical heating and cooking is harvested unsustainably.

definition.text: Biofuels are classed as first-generation, made from food crops on arable land, or second-generation, made from non-food biomass.

facts.text: First-generation biofuels come from crops such as sugarcane and maize; bioethanol is fermented from their sugars or starch and is widely used in the United States and Brazil.
Biodiesel comes from oils such as rapeseed and is the most common biofuel in Europe.
Second-generation or advanced biofuels use perennial energy crops and agricultural residues, grown as by-products of a main crop or on marginal land.

title: Surface power density
article: Bioenergy#Comparison with other renewable energy types

definition.text: Surface power density is the power a generation source delivers per square metre of land, which fixes how much land a given supply needs.

facts.text: One estimate of lifecycle surface power density is 0.30 W/m2 for biomass, 1 for wind, 3 for hydro and 5 for solar.
Lifecycle density counts land used by supporting infrastructure, manufacturing, mining or harvesting, and decommissioning.
Another estimate gives medians of 0.08 W/m2 for biomass, 0.14 hydro, 1.84 wind and 6.63 solar, none above 10 W/m2.

definition.text: Water pollution is the contamination of water bodies, usually by human activity, in a way that harms how they can be used.

facts.text: Water bodies include surface water such as lakes, rivers, oceans and reservoirs, and also groundwater.
Water counts as polluted when it can no longer serve a use such as drinking, or when its ability to support fish and other biota has changed significantly.

Main contaminant groups are pathogens, organic compounds such as petroleum hydrocarbons, inorganic ones such as heavy metals, nitrates, phosphates and silt, pharmaceuticals, and solid waste and plastics.

Point sources are single identifiable outlets such as sewage plants and factories; nonpoint pollution is diffuse, the summed effect of small amounts from a large area, and agriculture is a major contributor.
A 2017 study said polluted water spread gastrointestinal diseases and parasitic infections and killed 1.8 million people.
Nutrient pollution is a primary cause of eutrophication, where excess nitrogen or phosphorus stimulates algal growth.
Regulation is only part of the answer; education, economic instruments, market forces and stricter enforcement are also needed.

definition.text: Thermal pollution is the degradation of water quality by human activity that raises or lowers a water body's ambient temperature.

facts.text: Temperature is one of the physical changes that, with chemicals and pathogens, can degrade aquatic ecosystems.

definition.text: Water pollution is controlled by treating municipal, industrial and agricultural wastewater and by managing sediment and urban runoff at the source.

facts.text: Municipal wastewater can be treated in centralized plants, decentralized systems, nature-based solutions or septic tanks; waste stabilization ponds are a low-cost option.
Treated industrial effluent may be reused or released to a sanitary sewer or surface water.
Construction sediment is managed with erosion controls such as mulching and sediment controls such as basins and silt fences.
Controlling urban runoff means slowing stormwater flow and cutting pollutant discharges.
In the United States the 1972 Clean Water Act amendments set up the main framework for improving water quality in surface waters.

definition.text: A commodity is an economic good, usually a resource, whose instances the market treats as equivalent regardless of who produced them (fungibility).

facts.text: Most commodities are raw materials, agricultural or mining products such as iron ore, sugar, rice and wheat; crude oil, corn and gold are popular ones.
Price is set by the whole market, and established physical commodities have actively traded spot and derivative markets.
Wide availability means smaller profit margins and makes factors other than price, such as brand, matter less.
Soft commodities are grown goods like wheat or rice; hard ones include gold, silver and oil; energy commodities include electricity, gas, coal and oil.
On an exchange the contract's underlying standard defines the commodity, not any quality of a particular producer's product.
Commoditization is a spectrum: even electricity can be differentiated by generation method where buyers can pay more for renewables.
Some customers differentiate on sustainability or animal welfare, so organic, cage-free or Forest Stewardship Council labels separate otherwise commodity goods.

definition.text: A commodity super cycle is a period of about a decade when commodities as a whole trade above their long-term moving average.

facts.text: A super cycle usually follows large industrial or commercial change that demands more resources.
There have been four super cycles in the last 120 years; the latest began in 2000 as China joined the WTO and was halted by the 2008 recession.
A 1970s boom ended when foreign investment fled as extractive industries were nationalized.

contested_note: Proponents and opponents disagree on whether privatization improves services and who should provide public goods.
title: Privatization

definition.text: Privatization most commonly means moving something from the public sector into the private sector, such as selling a state-owned enterprise to private investors.

facts.text: It can also mean deregulation of a heavily regulated private industry, or contracting out government functions like water supply, revenue collection or prison management.
Privatization gained worldwide momentum in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher in the UK and Ronald Reagan in the US.
Governments tend to privatize more when public debt is higher, and when they cannot fund investment needed for profitability.
World Bank and Megginson research in the early 2000s found privatization in competitive industries with well-informed consumers consistently improved efficiency.
Outcomes vary by privatization model, and it is hard to separate its effects from wider economic trends.
Proponents expect lower prices, better quality and less corruption, but concede market failures and natural monopolies may be problematic.
Opponents hold that public goods and services should stay with government so everyone has access, and that natural monopolies are better run by the state.

definition.text: Privatization takes several main forms: share issue, asset sale, voucher privatization, privatization from below and management buyout.

facts.text: Share issue sells the enterprise's shares on the stock market; asset sale divests to a strategic investor, usually by auction.
Voucher privatization gives citizens vouchers for part ownership of a corporation, usually free or very cheap.
Privatization from below is the start of new private businesses in formerly socialist countries; a management buyout lets managers buy public shares.
Some sales, like Chicago's 2008 75-year parking meter deal, are criticised as secured borrowing that lets politicians raise money without taxes or debt.

definition.text: Trade is the exchange of something of value for something else of value, pre-agreed as a contract.

facts.text: Trade exists because of specialization and division of labour, as people concentrate on a small part of production and trade their output.
Regions trade because they have a comparative advantage in some goods, including scarce natural resources found elsewhere.
Prehistoric people exchanged goods in a gift economy before currency; evidence includes obsidian networks 15,000 years ago and ostrich eggshell beads 50,000 years ago.
The 1944 Bretton Woods Agreement set up the IMF and the World Bank to regulate the international economy and prevent national trade barriers.
International trade has helped develop the world economy but, with agreements lowering tariffs, has sometimes harmed local-product markets in poorer countries.
South Korea's export-oriented industrialization did much better than India's historically closed policy, though effective state institutions also mattered.

definition.text: Free trade is a policy by which a government does not discriminate against imports or exports through tariffs or subsidies.

facts.text: Free trade does not mean a country abandons all control and taxation of imports and exports.
In 1992 the European Union lifted barriers to internal trade in goods and labour.
The WTO's Doha round aimed to lower trade barriers with a focus on fairness for developing countries; agricultural subsidies were the hardest issue to settle.

definition.text: Protectionism is the policy of restraining and discouraging trade between states, often through tariffs and restrictive quotas.

facts.text: Protectionist policies were particularly prevalent in the 1930s, between the Great Depression and World War II.
Mill argued a country with monopoly pricing power could manipulate its terms of trade through tariffs, which was taken as evidence against a universal doctrine of free trade.
Mill's infant industry argument holds that government should protect young industries only as long as they need to reach full capacity, and many industrializing countries adopted it.

Most economists reject protection for unemployment, national defence and self-sufficiency (autarky) arguments, and overwhelmingly reject the view that bilateral trade deficits are harmful in themselves.

definition.text: Trade sanctions are restrictions imposed on a country to punish it for an action, the severest being an embargo, a blockade of all trade.

facts.text: Embargoes are usually temporary; the US embargo on Cuba has lasted over 60 years.

definition.text: Urban economics is a branch of microeconomics that studies urban spatial structure and the location of households and firms.

facts.text: Unlike most neoclassical economics it focuses on spatial relationships, and it is rooted in the location theories of von Thünen, Alonso, Christaller and Lösch.
It asks why cities develop where they do, why some are large and small, what drives growth and decline, and why land prices vary across space.
O'Sullivan divides it into six themes: market forces in city development, land use, urban transportation, urban problems, housing policy and local government expenditure.
Most urban economics today is neoclassical and centred on experiences in the Global North.

definition.text: Urbanization is the process by which settlements grow as more people live and work in cities, shifting population from rural to urban areas.

facts.text: It refers to the proportion of a national population living in urban areas, not the absolute number of urban dwellers.
The rural-urban balance stayed near a fixed equilibrium until the British Agricultural and Industrial Revolutions broke it in the late 18th century.
Cities offer labour-market access, education, housing and lower commuting costs, but also stress, higher living costs and marginalization.
Global urban area more than doubled from 33 Mha in 1992 to 71 Mha in 2015, consuming 24 Mha of fertile cropland and 3.3 Mha of forest.
Impervious surfaces send untreated runoff to streams and coasts instead of groundwater, and fragmentation of habitats by roads and railways harms biodiversity.
Global urbanization averaged 56.2% in 2020, with very low urbanization in belts across central-eastern Africa and central-southeast Asia.
Planned urbanization follows an advance plan, as in the garden city movement; suburbanization shifts residential areas outward.
